subject: Everyday Science
q: The fluid part of blood is known as:
explanation: Plasma is the pale yellow liquid, mostly water, in which blood cells, nutrients, hormones and wastes are carried.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The life span of red blood cells in humans is about:
explanation: Red blood cells circulate for roughly 120 days before worn-out cells are removed, mainly by the spleen.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which blood group is known as the universal donor?
explanation: O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens, so they can be given in emergencies to recipients of any blood group.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A person with blood group AB positive can receive red cells of any ABO group because his plasma has:
explanation: Transfused red cells are attacked only if the recipient's plasma has matching antibodies; AB people carry neither anti-A nor anti-B.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying pigment of red blood cells, contains:
explanation: Each haemoglobin unit has an iron-containing haem group that binds oxygen; this is why iron deficiency causes anaemia.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which blood component helps the blood to clot at a wound?
explanation: Platelets are cell fragments that stick together at a damaged vessel and start the clotting process.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The main function of white blood cells is to:
explanation: White blood cells engulf germs or produce antibodies, forming the core of the immune defence.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In adults, red blood cells are produced mainly in the:
explanation: After birth, blood cells are formed in the red marrow of bones such as the ribs, sternum, vertebrae and pelvis.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Old and worn-out red blood cells are mainly broken down in the:
explanation: The spleen filters the blood and removes aged red cells, which is why it is sometimes called the graveyard of red blood cells.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Mature human red blood cells lack a:
explanation: Human red cells lose their nucleus as they mature, leaving more room for haemoglobin; this is also why they cannot divide.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An average adult human body contains about how much blood?
explanation: An adult has roughly 5 litres of blood, about 7–8 per cent of body weight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest artery in the human body is the:
explanation: The aorta leaves the left ventricle and distributes oxygenated blood to the whole body through its branches.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so they have thick, muscular walls.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
explanation: The pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood; it takes blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body?
explanation: The left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall because it pumps blood through the aorta to the entire body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The natural pacemaker of the heart is the:
explanation: The SA node in the right atrium sends out the electrical impulses that set the rhythm of each heartbeat.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The normal resting blood pressure of a healthy adult is about:
explanation: 120 is the systolic pressure when the heart contracts and 80 the diastolic pressure when it relaxes.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The average resting heart rate of a healthy adult is about:
explanation: A normal resting rate lies between 60 and 100 beats per minute, with about 72 usually quoted as average.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Veins have valves in order to:
explanation: Blood in veins flows under low pressure, so valves keep it moving towards the heart, especially from the legs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Exchange of gases and nutrients between blood and body tissues takes place through the:
explanation: Capillary walls are only one cell thick, allowing oxygen and nutrients to pass out and wastes to pass in.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The "lub-dub" sounds of the heartbeat are produced by:
explanation: The first sound comes from the closing of the valves between atria and ventricles, the second from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The circulation of blood was first accurately described by:
explanation: The English physician William Harvey showed in 1628 that the heart pumps blood round the body in a continuous circuit.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest gland in the human body is the:
explanation: The liver is the largest internal organ and gland; it makes bile, stores glycogen and detoxifies substances.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the:
explanation: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile and releases it into the small intestine after a fatty meal.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bile helps digestion by:
explanation: Bile salts emulsify fats, giving fat-digesting enzymes (lipases) a much larger surface to work on.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Most digestion and absorption of food takes place in the:
explanation: Enzymes from the pancreas and intestinal wall complete digestion in the small intestine, whose villi then absorb the products.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The finger-like villi of the small intestine help by:
o: Increasing the surface area for absorption
explanation: Millions of villi greatly enlarge the absorbing surface, so digested food passes quickly into the blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The acid secreted in the human stomach is:
explanation: Gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, which kills many germs and provides the acidic conditions pepsin needs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Digestion of starch begins in the:
explanation: Saliva contains the enzyme amylase, which starts breaking starch into sugars while food is being chewed.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Protein digestion begins in the stomach through the action of the enzyme:
explanation: Pepsin works in the acidic stomach to break proteins into smaller peptides.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The main function of the large intestine is to absorb:
explanation: Nutrients are absorbed earlier in the small intestine; the large intestine reclaims water and salts and forms faeces.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In the human body, extra glucose is stored in the liver and muscles as:
explanation: Animals store carbohydrate as glycogen, which the liver can break down to release glucose when blood sugar falls; starch is the plant store.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In the lungs, exchange of gases takes place in the:
explanation: Alveoli are tiny thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries, where oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves the blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: When we breathe in, the diaphragm:
o: Pushes air out of the lungs
explanation: Contraction flattens the diaphragm, enlarging the chest cavity so air is drawn into the lungs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which structure prevents food from entering the windpipe during swallowing?
explanation: The epiglottis is a flap of cartilage that closes over the entrance of the larynx when we swallow.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The voice box in humans is the:
explanation: The larynx contains the vocal cords, which vibrate as air passes to produce sound.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Oxygen passes from the alveoli into the blood by:
explanation: Oxygen moves from high concentration in the alveolar air to lower concentration in the blood, which is diffusion.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Each kidney is made up of about a million tiny filtering units called:
explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, which filter blood and form urine.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Urea, the main nitrogenous waste in humans, is produced in the:
explanation: The liver converts toxic ammonia from protein breakdown into urea; the kidneys only remove it from the blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The kidneys remove wastes from the body by:
explanation: Kidneys filter wastes such as urea and excess salts and water out of the blood to form urine.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Haemodialysis is a treatment used for failure of the:
explanation: A dialysis machine filters wastes and excess fluid from the blood when the kidneys can no longer do so.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:
explanation: Neurons are nerve cells that carry electrical impulses; synapses are only the junctions between them.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which part of the brain controls thinking, memory and voluntary actions?
explanation: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and is responsible for intelligence, memory, speech and voluntary movement.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Balance and coordination of body movements are controlled by the:
explanation: The cerebellum at the back of the brain fine-tunes posture, balance and smooth muscular movement.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Involuntary actions such as breathing and heartbeat are controlled by the:
explanation: The medulla in the brainstem regulates vital automatic functions such as breathing rate, heart rate and blood pressure.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A reflex action, such as quickly pulling the hand away from a hot object, is controlled mainly by the:
explanation: In a reflex arc the impulse is routed through the spinal cord, producing a response before the brain is consciously aware.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Body temperature in humans is regulated by the:
explanation: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat, triggering sweating or shivering to keep temperature near 37 °C.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which gland is known as the "master gland" of the body?
explanation: The pituitary secretes hormones that control several other endocrine glands, such as the thyroid and adrenals.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make the hormone:
explanation: Thyroxine, which controls the rate of metabolism, contains iodine; lack of iodine enlarges the thyroid (goitre).

subject: Everyday Science
q: Insulin is secreted by the:
explanation: Insulin is made by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Insulin lowers the blood sugar level by:
o: Helping body cells take up glucose
explanation: Insulin signals muscle, liver and fat cells to absorb glucose from the blood and store the excess as glycogen.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pancreatic hormone that raises the blood glucose level when it falls too low is:
explanation: Glucagon makes the liver break down glycogen into glucose, balancing the effect of insulin.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which hormone prepares the body for "fight or flight" in an emergency?
explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands raises heart rate, breathing and blood sugar to prepare the body for sudden action.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The hormone melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle, is produced by the:
explanation: The pineal gland releases melatonin mainly in darkness, signalling the body that it is time to sleep.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Hormones reach their target organs through the:
explanation: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones directly into the bloodstream, which carries them round the body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which organ works both as an endocrine gland and as an exocrine gland?
explanation: The pancreas releases insulin and glucagon into the blood and also sends digestive enzymes through a duct to the intestine.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An adult human skeleton normally has:
explanation: A newborn has about 300 bones, but many fuse during growth, leaving 206 in the adult.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The longest bone in the human body is the:
explanation: The femur, or thigh bone, is also the strongest bone and bears the body's weight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The smallest bone in the human body, the stapes, is found in the:
explanation: The stapes is one of three tiny middle-ear bones that pass sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.

subject: Everyday Science
q: At joints, bones are held together by:
explanation: Ligaments are tough, slightly elastic bands that connect bone to bone and stabilise joints.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Muscles are attached to bones by:
explanation: Tendons are strong, inelastic cords that transmit the pull of a contracting muscle to the bone.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The shoulder joint is an example of a:
explanation: The rounded head of the humerus fits into a socket, allowing movement in almost every direction.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cardiac muscle is found only in the:
explanation: Cardiac muscle contracts rhythmically without tiring and is found only in the wall of the heart.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The hardest substance in the human body is:
explanation: Enamel, the outer layer of the tooth crown, is highly mineralised and harder than bone.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A full set of permanent teeth in an adult human numbers:
explanation: Adults have 32 permanent teeth including four wisdom teeth; children have 20 milk teeth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The light-sensitive layer of the eye on which images are formed is the:
explanation: The retina contains rods and cones that convert light into nerve impulses sent to the brain through the optic nerve.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The size of the pupil is controlled by the:
explanation: The muscular, coloured iris widens or narrows the pupil to regulate how much light enters the eye.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In dim light, the pupil of the eye:
o: Widens to let in more light
explanation: Muscles of the iris enlarge the pupil in darkness so that more light reaches the retina.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which cells in the retina enable us to see colours?
explanation: Cones work in bright light and detect colour; rods are more sensitive in dim light but do not distinguish colours.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Short-sightedness (myopia) is corrected by using:
explanation: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina; a diverging concave lens moves it back onto the retina.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The part of the inner ear that converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses is the:
explanation: The coiled, fluid-filled cochlea contains hair cells that turn vibrations into signals for the auditory nerve.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the:
explanation: By linking the middle ear with the throat, the tube equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which part of the ear helps maintain the balance of the body?
explanation: The fluid-filled semicircular canals of the inner ear sense head movement and send balance information to the brain.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest organ of the human body is the:
explanation: The skin covers the whole body and protects it, regulates temperature and senses touch.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pigment that gives colour to human skin and protects it from ultraviolet rays is:
explanation: Melanin absorbs harmful UV radiation; people with more melanin have darker skin.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sweating helps to cool the body because:
o: Evaporation of sweat takes heat away from the skin
Sweat reduces blood flow to the skin
explanation: Evaporating water absorbs heat, so sweat drawing heat from the skin as it evaporates lowers body temperature.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Antibodies are produced by:
explanation: B lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, make antibodies that recognise and neutralise specific germs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Roughly what proportion of an adult human body's weight is water?
explanation: Water makes up around 60 per cent of an adult's body weight, found inside cells, in blood and in tissue fluid.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The longest cell in the human body is the:
explanation: Some nerve cells have axons running from the spinal cord to the toes, about a metre long.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The normal temperature of the human body is about:
explanation: A healthy body is kept close to 37 °C (98.6 °F); a temperature well above this indicates fever.
